corrected_value.title: The acquisition of abstract words by young infants.

decisions.quote: While the study was not designed to test the difference between noun and verb acquisition, 6–9-month-olds did perform well on one of the two verb pairs ( hug - eat ), contrary to their poor performance on a broader set of non-nouns in a prior study ( Bergelson & Swingley, 2013 ). Whether infants’ apparent success on hug-eat represents random item variation, or a first fragile glimmer of infants’ understanding of these verbs, is unclear, particularly given infants’ failure to demonstrate understanding of kiss-drink here.
decisions.reason: The replicating study empirically re-tests findings from Bergelson & Swingley (2013b) (DOI 10.1016/j.cognition.2013.02.011) in a new sample of 6–16-month-old infants using paired dynamic video stimuli: it explicitly repeats the hug-eat verb pair tested in Bergelson & Swingley (2013b), tests whether 6–9-month-olds' prior failure on non-nouns in that dynamic-video study was due to dynamic video presentation versus word class, and re-tests the non-linear comprehension boost around 13–14 months reported in both Bergelson & Swingley (2012) and (2013b). Both the Works Cited list and Crossref metadata verify the identity of Bergelson & Swingley (2013b) in Cognition 127(3), 391–397. The sole shipped original (input_row_index 391, Bergelson & Swingley, 2012, DOI 10.1073/pnas.1113380109) is a separate PNAS article testing concrete food and body-part nouns with static images, and sibling missing target_index 4 (Tincoff & Jusczyk, 2012, DOI 10.1111/j.1532-7078.2011.00084.x) is a distinct Infancy study on body-part nouns; report equivalence does not apply. Prior adjudication and state files were checked and are absent for this work.
